subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on organic chemistry, then mark my answer against the CCEA spec.
promptWeak: Explain organic chemistry for GCSE CCEA Chemistry simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: A hydrocarbon is a compound containing:
questions.explain: A hydrocarbon contains only the elements hydrogen and carbon.

options: A compound of carbon and oxygen
questions.explain: Crude oil is a mixture of many different hydrocarbons formed over millions of years.

questions.q: Crude oil is separated into useful fractions by:
questions.explain: Fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions with similar boiling points.

questions.q: In a fractionating column, fractions with the highest boiling points are collected:
questions.explain: Larger molecules have higher boiling points and condense low down where it is hottest; smaller molecules rise higher before condensing.

questions.q: A homologous series is a family of compounds that share:
options: The same general formula and similar chemical properties
questions.explain: Members of a homologous series have the same general formula, the same functional group and similar chemical properties, with a gradual change in physical properties.

questions.q: What is the general formula of the alkanes?
questions.explain: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CnH2n+2, e.g. methane CH4, ethane C2H6.

questions.q: Alkanes are described as saturated because they contain:
questions.explain: Saturated means only single C-C bonds; no more atoms can be added across the bonds.

questions.q: Which is the formula of propane?
questions.explain: Propane has 3 carbons: CnH2n+2 gives C3H(2x3+2) = C3H8.

questions.q: What are the products of the complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
questions.explain: Complete combustion (plenty of oxygen) produces carbon dioxide and water.

questions.q: Incomplete combustion of a hydrocarbon can produce which toxic gas?
questions.explain: With a limited oxygen supply, incomplete combustion can produce carbon monoxide (a toxic gas) and carbon (soot).

options: Join small molecules into large ones
Break long-chain hydrocarbons into smaller, more useful molecules
questions.explain: Cracking breaks long-chain alkanes into shorter, more useful hydrocarbons, including alkenes.

questions.q: The products of cracking a long alkane always include:
options: A shorter alkane and an alkene
questions.explain: Cracking produces a shorter-chain alkane and at least one alkene, e.g. C10H22 -> C8H18 + C2H4.

questions.q: What is the general formula of the alkenes?
questions.explain: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with a C=C double bond and general formula CnH2n, e.g. ethene C2H4.

questions.q: Alkenes are described as unsaturated because they contain:
questions.explain: Alkenes contain at least one C=C double bond, so they are unsaturated and can undergo addition reactions.

questions.q: When bromine water is shaken with an alkene, the colour change observed is:
questions.explain: Alkenes decolourise bromine water: the orange bromine water turns colourless. Alkanes give no change (stays orange).

questions.q: In addition polymerisation, the monomers must contain:
questions.explain: Addition polymerisation joins many alkene (unsaturated) monomers; the C=C double bonds open up to form long saturated chains, e.g. ethene -> poly(ethene).

questions.q: What is the functional group of the alcohols?
questions.explain: Alcohols contain the -OH (hydroxyl) functional group, e.g. ethanol C2H5OH.

questions.q: What is the molecular formula of ethanol?
questions.explain: Ethanol has 2 carbons and the -OH group: C2H5OH (which can be written C2H6O).

questions.q: What is the functional group of the carboxylic acids?
questions.explain: Carboxylic acids contain the -COOH functional group, e.g. ethanoic acid CH3COOH, and are weak acids in water.
